extracted.intended_audience: novice and experienced TeX users; authors/typesetters preparing technical or mathematical manuscripts
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and conventions for preparing high-quality technical (especially mathematical) manuscripts with TeX; covers input conventions, fonts, control sequences, spacing, and higher-level formatting practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Goal: produce the finest quality technical manuscripts
rubrics_metrics.description: "This is a handbook about TEX, a new typesetting system intended for the creation of beautiful books—and especially for books that contain a lot of mathematics."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use TeX when the goal is highest typographic quality; producing such quality requires more attention to detail than simpler systems do. If you merely want passably good output, a simpler system may suffice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reading-level signposting: "dangerous bend" for wizard-only material
rubrics_metrics.description: When the symbol (dangerous bend) appears at the beginning of a paragraph, it warns of a “dangerous bend” in the train of thought; don’t read the paragraph unless you need to.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat paragraphs marked with one dangerous-bend sign as optional advanced material; double signs indicate material intended only for experienced users (skip on first/second reading).

rubrics_metrics.name: Exercises: attempt before consulting answers
rubrics_metrics.description: "EXERCISES are sprinkled through this manual. It is generally intended that every reader should try every exercise... If you can’t solve a problem, you can always look up the answer. But please, try first to solve it by yourself; then you’ll learn more and you’ll learn faster."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work exercises to internalize material; check Appendix A for answers only after effort. Dangerous-bend exercises are exceptions for less experienced readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quotation marks: type two single-quotes for double quotes
rubrics_metrics.description: To produce double-quote marks with TeX, type two single-quote marks of the appropriate kind. Example: to get “I understand.” type ‘‘I understand.’’.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If keyboard lacks left-quote, use control sequences \lq and \rq; for quotes within quotes or awkward combinations use \thinspace between adjacent quotes as shown (e.g., ’\thinspace’’ yields proper adjacent-quote spacing).

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyphen / en-dash / em-dash / minus: distinct characters and input conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: In good math books these symbols are all different: a hyphen (-); an en-dash (--); an em-dash (---); a minus sign ($-$ in math mode).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use '-' for hyphenation (compound words), '--' for ranges/pages (en-dash), '---' for punctuation/em-dash, and math-mode '-' ($-$) for minus signs. Be conscientious about using the correct one.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ligatures and kerning are automatic
rubrics_metrics.description: Professional typesetters use ligatures for letter combinations like ff, fi, fl, ffi, ffl; TeX handles such things automatically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not manually substitute ligatures or kerning adjustments in normal text; TeX will take care of ligatures and kerning (and it also converts sequences like '--' to an en-dash).

rubrics_metrics.name: Escape character and control-sequence categories
rubrics_metrics.description: The backslash '\' is used as the escape character. Control sequences come in two flavors: control words (escape + letters) and control symbols (escape + single nonletter).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After a control word a following space is ignored (so use a control space '\ ' to force a real space); control symbols need no separating space. Digits are not letters for control-word parsing. Understand these rules to avoid surprising tokenization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spaces: consecutive spaces collapse and control-space '\ ' to force a space
rubrics_metrics.description: TeX treats two or more consecutive spaces as a single space; a space after a control word is ignored unless you force it with control space ('\ ').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely on typing multiple spaces for formatting; use TeX spacing commands or explicit control-space where needed. Nonprinting control characters like \hreturni and \htabi are treated like control space and should not be redefined.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use grouping { } for local font changes
rubrics_metrics.description: It's a nuisance to say '\rm' every time you want to go back to roman, so use grouping: e.g., 'to be {\bf bold} or to {\sl emphasize} something.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer local grouping with { } for temporary font/style changes rather than globally switching fonts and then trying to restore them; this makes manuscripts more natural and less error-prone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Italic/slanted to roman correction: use \/ (italic correction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Because italic and slanted styles slope, letters stick into following spaces; put the special control sequence '\/' just before switching back to unslanted letters to add an 'italic correction'. Example: '{\it italicized\/} and {\sl slanted\/} words'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use \/ when switching from italic/slanted to roman or bold (so spacing looks correct); standard rule: use \/ unless the next character is a period or comma. Remember to use it even for bold 'f' as in '{\bf f\/}'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Font usage and sizes: limited use of special faces and named font macros
rubrics_metrics.description: Plain TeX provides \rm, \sl, \it, \tt, \bf to select roman, slanted, italic, typewriter, and bold faces. Fonts vary in size (e.g., 10-point = \tenrm) and have matching slanted/roman pairs (\tensl, \ninerm, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reserve special fonts for emphasis; roman should be main text for readability. Use named font size macros (e.g., \tenrm, \ninerm) consistently. Avoid overusing emphasis faces for sustained reading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer higher-level control sequences/macros over primitives
rubrics_metrics.description: About 300 of TeX's control sequences are primitives; others are defined. People hardly ever use primitives in manuscripts; higher-level control sequences are easier and less error-prone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define or use macros (formats) for recurring complex formatting. Use \show\cs to inspect a control sequence's current meaning (shows whether primitive or macro). Start with plain TeX definitions and adapt rather than coding primitives repeatedly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plain TeX as a baseline format and modifiability
rubrics_metrics.description: Plain TeX is a set of about 600 basic control sequences (Appendix B). Plain TeX is only one of countless formats that can be designed on top of TeX's primitives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rely on plain TeX as a starting point; modify definitions gradually to achieve custom formats. Appendix E contains example formats including the format used to typeset this manual.

rubrics_metrics.name: Macro encapsulation for document-level constructs (example: \exercise)
rubrics_metrics.description: High-level control sequences govern overall document format. The \exercise command performs many tasks: compute exercise number, typeset heading/triangle, leave/suppress space, prevent undesirable page breaks, suppress indentation, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encapsulate repeated document-format behaviors in macros so a single change to the macro reflows the entire document consistently; avoid repeating low-level instructions throughout the manuscript.

rubrics_metrics.name: Logo and spacing: careful handling of \TeX and following spaces
rubrics_metrics.description: The \TeX control sequence produces the logo; TeX ignores spaces after control words, so an extra '\ ' (control space) is often required: '\TeX\ ignores spaces after control words.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use control space after logo/macro when a normal interword space is desired. Beware of adding a stray '\' when the following character could turn it into another control sequence (example: 'the logo ‘\TeX\'.' makes '\\'' become an accent sequence and yields an accented period).

rubrics_metrics.name: Adjacent-quote spacing: use \thinspace between single and double quotes
rubrics_metrics.description: To get a single quote followed by a double quote to appear nicely (’ ”) type '’\thinspace’’'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid using visible normal spaces between adjacent quotes (that creates too-large spacing) and avoid naive constructs that TeX will misinterpret; \thinspace gives the visually correct small spacing between adjacent quote marks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accents as control symbols (\' and \" etc.) and their usage
rubrics_metrics.description: Control sequences like \' and \" are control symbols used to place accents: 'George P\'olya' yields 'George P´olya', and 'Gabor Szeg\"o' yields 'Gabor Szeg¨o.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use accent control symbols directly before the letter to be accented; remember control-symbol parsing rules (single nonletter after backslash).

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not redefine special nonprinting control-space-like tokens
rubrics_metrics.description: Nonprinting control characters like \hreturni and \htabi are initially set up to behave like control space (\ ), and these special control sequences should probably not be redefined, because you can’t see the difference when viewing files.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid redefining \hreturni and \htabi; treat these as equivalent to control space in manuscripts to prevent mysterious spacing behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Whitespace and typing conventions: don't rely on typist two-space convention
rubrics_metrics.description: Typists are often taught to put two spaces at the ends of sentences; TeX has its own way to produce extra space in such cases, so you needn’t be consistent in the number of spaces you type.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Let TeX handle sentence spacing; do not insert extra spaces to force visual spacing. Understand TeX's sentence/space factor rules if precise spacing control is needed.
